# concurrent_queue - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/concurrent-queue/^2/

## Expand description

A concurrent multi-producer multi-consumer queue.

There are two kinds of queues:

Queues also have the capability to get [closed](https://docs.rs/struct.ConcurrentQueue.html#method.close) at any point. When closed, no more items can be
pushed into the queue, although the remaining items can still be popped.

These features make it easy to build channels similar to [ std::sync::mpsc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/sync/mpsc/index.html) on top of this
crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use concurrent_queue::ConcurrentQueue;
let q = ConcurrentQueue::unbounded();
q.push(1).unwrap();
q.push(2).unwrap();
assert_eq!(q.pop(), Ok(1));
assert_eq!(q.pop(), Ok(2));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

`concurrent-queue` uses an `std` default feature. With this feature enabled, this crate will
use [ std::thread::yield_now](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/thread/functions/fn.yield_now.html) to avoid busy waiting in tight loops. However, with this
feature disabled,

[will be used instead. Disabling](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hint/fn.spin_loop.html)

`core::hint::spin_loop``std` will allow
this crate to be used on `no_std` platforms at the potential expense of more busy waiting.There is also a `portable-atomic` feature, which uses a polyfill from the
[ portable-atomic](https://crates.io/crates/portable-atomic) crate to provide atomic operations on platforms that do not support them.
See the

[for the](https://github.com/taiki-e/portable-atomic/blob/main/README.md#optional-cfg)

`README`[crate for more information on how to use it. Note that even with this feature enabled,](https://crates.io/crates/portable-atomic)

`portable-atomic``concurrent-queue` still requires a global allocator
to be available. See the documentation for the [trait for more information.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/alloc/global/trait.GlobalAlloc.html)

`std::alloc::GlobalAlloc`## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Concurrent](https://docs.rs/struct.ConcurrentQueue.html)- Queue
- A concurrent queue.
- [Force](https://docs.rs/struct.ForcePushError.html)- Push - Error
- Error that occurs when force-pushing into a full queue.
- [TryIter](https://docs.rs/struct.TryIter.html)
- An iterator that pops items from a `ConcurrentQueue`

# event_listener - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/event-listener/^2.4.0/

## Expand description

Notify async tasks or threads.

This is a synchronization primitive similar to [eventcounts](http://www.1024cores.net/home/lock-free-algorithms/eventcounts) invented by Dmitry Vyukov.

You can use this crate to turn non-blocking data structures into async or blocking data
structures. See a [simple mutex](https://github.com/smol-rs/event-listener/blob/master/examples/mutex.rs) implementation that exposes an async and a blocking interface
for acquiring locks.

Wait until another thread sets a boolean flag:

```
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicBool, Ordering};
use std::sync::Arc;
use std::thread;
use std::time::Duration;
use std::usize;
use event_listener::Event;
let flag = Arc::new(AtomicBool::new(false));
let event = Arc::new(Event::new());
// Spawn a thread that will set the flag after 1 second.
thread::spawn({
    let flag = flag.clone();
    let event = event.clone();
    move || {
        // Wait for a second.
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_secs(1));
        // Set the flag.
        flag.store(true, Ordering::SeqCst);
        // Notify all listeners that the flag has been set.
        event.notify(usize::MAX);
    }
});
// Wait until the flag is set.
loop {
    // Check the flag.
    if flag.load(Ordering::SeqCst) {
        break;
    }
    // Start listening for events.
    let listener = event.listen();
    // Check the flag again after creating the listener.
    if flag.load(Ordering::SeqCst) {
        break;
    }
    // Wait for a notification and continue the loop.
    listener.wait();
}
```

# easy_parallel - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/easy-parallel/^3/

## Expand description

Run closures in parallel.

This is a simple primitive for spawning threads in bulk and waiting for them to complete. Threads are allowed to borrow local variables from the main thread.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Run two threads that increment a number:

```
use easy_parallel::Parallel;
use std::sync::Mutex;
let mut m = Mutex::new(0);
Parallel::new()
    .add(|| *m.lock().unwrap() += 1)
    .add(|| *m.lock().unwrap() += 1)
    .run();
assert_eq!(*m.get_mut().unwrap(), 2);
```
Square each number of a vector on a different thread:

```
use easy_parallel::Parallel;
let v = vec![10, 20, 30];
let squares = Parallel::new()
    .each(0..v.len(), |i| v[i] * v[i])
    .run();
assert_eq!(squares, [100, 400, 900]);
```
Compute the sum of numbers in an array:

```
use easy_parallel::Parallel;
fn par_sum(v: &[i32]) -> i32 {
    const THRESHOLD: usize = 2;
    if v.len() <= THRESHOLD {
        v.iter().copied().sum()
    } else {
        let half = (v.len() + 1) / 2;
        let sums = Parallel::new().each(v.chunks(half), par_sum).run();
        sums.into_iter().sum()
    }
}
let v = [1, 25, -4, 10, 8];
assert_eq!(par_sum(&v), 40);
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Parallel](https://docs.rs/struct.Parallel.html)
- A builder that runs closures in parallel.

# futures_lite - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/futures-lite/^1/

## Expand description

Futures, streams, and async I/O combinators.

This crate is a subset of [futures](https://docs.rs/futures) that compiles an order of magnitude faster, fixes minor
warts in its API, fills in some obvious gaps, and removes almost all unsafe code from it.

In short, this crate aims to be more enjoyable than [futures](https://docs.rs/futures) but still fully compatible with
it.

```
use futures_lite::future;
fn main() {
    future::block_on(async {
        println!("Hello world!");
    })
}
```
- Tools and combinators for I/O.

- Pins a variable of type`T`on the stack and rebinds it as`Pin<&mut T>`.

# async_channel - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/async-channel/latest/target-redirect/async_channel/

## Expand description

An async multi-producer multi-consumer channel, where each message can be received by only one of all existing consumers.

There are two kinds of channels:

A channel has the [ Sender](https://docs.rs/struct.Sender.html) and

[side. Both sides are cloneable and can be shared among multiple threads.](https://docs.rs/struct.Receiver.html)

`Receiver`When all [ Sender](https://docs.rs/struct.Sender.html)s or all

[s are dropped, the channel becomes closed. When a channel is closed, no more messages can be sent, but remaining messages can still be received.](https://docs.rs/struct.Receiver.html)

`Receiver`The channel can also be closed manually by calling [ Sender::close()](https://docs.rs/struct.Sender.html#method.close) or

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Receiver.html#method.close)

`Receiver::close()`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
let (s, r) = async_channel::unbounded();
assert_eq!(s.send("Hello").await, Ok(()));
assert_eq!(r.recv().await, Ok("Hello"));
```

# async_channel - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/async-channel/1.9.0/target-redirect/i686-pc-windows-msvc/async_channel/

## Expand description

An async multi-producer multi-consumer channel, where each message can be received by only one of all existing consumers.

There are two kinds of channels:

A channel has the [ Sender](https://docs.rs/struct.Sender.html) and

[side. Both sides are cloneable and can be shared among multiple threads.](https://docs.rs/struct.Receiver.html)

`Receiver`When all [ Sender](https://docs.rs/struct.Sender.html)s or all

[s are dropped, the channel becomes closed. When a channel is closed, no more messages can be sent, but remaining messages can still be received.](https://docs.rs/struct.Receiver.html)

`Receiver`The channel can also be closed manually by calling [ Sender::close()](https://docs.rs/struct.Sender.html#method.close) or

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Receiver.html#method.close)

`Receiver::close()````
let (s, r) = async_channel::unbounded();
assert_eq!(s.send("Hello").await, Ok(()));
assert_eq!(r.recv().await, Ok("Hello"));
```
- The receiving side of a channel.
- The sending side of a channel.

- Creates a bounded channel.
- Creates an unbounded channel.

# bounded in async_channel - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/async-channel/^1.5.1/fn.bounded.html

## Expand description

Creates a bounded channel.

The created channel has space to hold at most `cap` messages at a time.

Capacity must be a positive number. If `cap` is zero, this function will panic.

```
use async_channel::{bounded, TryRecvError, TrySendError};
let (s, r) = bounded(1);
assert_eq!(s.send(10).await, Ok(()));
assert_eq!(s.try_send(20), Err(TrySendError::Full(20)));
assert_eq!(r.recv().await, Ok(10));
assert_eq!(r.try_recv(), Err(TryRecvError::Empty));
```

---

# unbounded in async_channel - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/async-channel/^1.5.1/fn.unbounded.html

## Expand description

Creates an unbounded channel.

The created channel can hold an unlimited number of messages.

```
use async_channel::{unbounded, TryRecvError};
let (s, r) = unbounded();
assert_eq!(s.send(10).await, Ok(()));
assert_eq!(s.send(20).await, Ok(()));
assert_eq!(r.recv().await, Ok(10));
assert_eq!(r.recv().await, Ok(20));
assert_eq!(r.try_recv(), Err(TryRecvError::Empty));
```

---

# Sender in async_channel - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/async-channel/^1.5.1/struct.Sender.html

`pub struct Sender<T> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The sending side of a channel.

Senders can be cloned and shared among threads. When all senders associated with a channel are dropped, the channel becomes closed.

The channel can also be closed manually by calling [ Sender::close()](https://docs.rs/struct.Sender.html#method.close).

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[source](https://docs.rs/src/async_channel/lib.rs.html#200-215)#### pub fn [try_send](https://docs.rs#method.try_send)(&self, msg: T) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [TrySendError](https://docs.rs/enum.TrySendError.html)<T>>

[source](https://docs.rs/src/async_channel/lib.rs.html#200-215)

#### pub fn [try_send](https://docs.rs#method.try_send)(&self, msg: T) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [TrySendError](https://docs.rs/enum.TrySendError.html)<T>>

Attempts to send a message into the channel.

If the channel is full or closed, this method returns an error.

```
use async_channel::{bounded, TrySendError};
let (s, r) = bounded(1);
assert_eq!(s.try_send(1), Ok(()));
assert_eq!(s.try_send(2), Err(TrySendError::Full(2)));
drop(r);
assert_eq!(s.try_send(3), Err(TrySendError::Closed(3)));
```
Sends a message into the channel.

If the channel is full, this method waits until there is space for a message.

If the channel is closed, this method returns an error.

```
use async_channel::{unbounded, SendError};
let (s, r) = unbounded();
assert_eq!(s.send(1).await, Ok(()));
drop(r);
assert_eq!(s.send(2).await, Err(SendError(2)));
```
[source](https://docs.rs/src/async_channel/lib.rs.html#269-271)#### pub fn [send_blocking](https://docs.rs#method.send_blocking)(&self, msg: T) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [SendError](https://docs.rs/struct.SendError.html)<T>>

[source](https://docs.rs/src/async_channel/lib.rs.html#269-271)

#### pub fn [send_blocking](https://docs.rs#method.send_blocking)(&self, msg: T) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [SendError](https://docs.rs/struct.SendError.html)<T>>

Sends a message into this channel using the blocking strategy.

If the channel is full, this method will block until there is room. If the channel is closed, this method returns an error.

Rather than using asynchronous waiting, like the [ send](https://docs.rs/struct.Sender.html#method.send) method,
this method will block the current thread until the message is sent.

This method should not be used in an asynchronous context. It is intended to be used such that a channel can be used in both asynchronous and synchronous contexts. Calling this method in an asynchronous context may result in deadlocks.

```
use async_channel::{unbounded, SendError};
let (s, r) = unbounded();
assert_eq!(s.send_blocking(1), Ok(()));
drop(r);
assert_eq!(s.send_blocking(2), Err(SendError(2)));
```
Closes the channel.

Returns `true` if this call has closed the channel and it was not closed already.

The remaining messages can still be received.

```
use async_channel::{unbounded, RecvError};
let (s, r) = unbounded();
assert_eq!(s.send(1).await, Ok(()));
assert!(s.close());
assert_eq!(r.recv().await, Ok(1));
assert_eq!(r.recv().await, Err(RecvError));
```
Returns the channel capacity if it’s bounded.

```
use async_channel::{bounded, unbounded};
let (s, r) = bounded::<i32>(5);
assert_eq!(s.capacity(), Some(5));
let (s, r) = unbounded::<i32>();
assert_eq!(s.capacity(), None);
```
[source](https://docs.rs/src/async_channel/lib.rs.html#408-410)#### pub fn [receiver_count](https://docs.rs#method.receiver_count)(&self) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)

[source](https://docs.rs/src/async_channel/lib.rs.html#408-410)

#### pub fn [receiver_count](https://docs.rs#method.receiver_count)(&self) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)

Returns the number of receivers for the channel.

```
use async_channel::unbounded;
let (s, r) = unbounded::<()>();
assert_eq!(s.receiver_count(), 1);
let r2 = r.clone();
assert_eq!(s.receiver_count(), 2);
```
[source](https://docs.rs/src/async_channel/lib.rs.html#427-429)#### pub fn [sender_count](https://docs.rs#method.sender_count)(&self) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)

[source](https://docs.rs/src/async_channel/lib.rs.html#427-429)

#### pub fn [sender_count](https://docs.rs#method.sender_count)(&self) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)

```

# Receiver in async_channel - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/async-channel/^1.5.1/struct.Receiver.html

`pub struct Receiver<T> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The receiving side of a channel.

Receivers can be cloned and shared among threads. When all receivers associated with a channel are dropped, the channel becomes closed.

The channel can also be closed manually by calling [ Receiver::close()](https://docs.rs/struct.Receiver.html#method.close).

Receivers implement the [ Stream](https://docs.rs/futures-core/0.3.28/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/futures_core/stream/trait.Stream.html) trait.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[source](https://docs.rs/src/async_channel/lib.rs.html#506-518)#### pub fn [try_recv](https://docs.rs#method.try_recv)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T, [TryRecvError](https://docs.rs/enum.TryRecvError.html)>

[source](https://docs.rs/src/async_channel/lib.rs.html#506-518)

#### pub fn [try_recv](https://docs.rs#method.try_recv)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T, [TryRecvError](https://docs.rs/enum.TryRecvError.html)>

Attempts to receive a message from the channel.

If the channel is empty, or empty and closed, this method returns an error.

```
use async_channel::{unbounded, TryRecvError};
let (s, r) = unbounded();
assert_eq!(s.send(1).await, Ok(()));
assert_eq!(r.try_recv(), Ok(1));
assert_eq!(r.try_recv(), Err(TryRecvError::Empty));
drop(s);
assert_eq!(r.try_recv(), Err(TryRecvError::Closed));
```
Receives a message from the channel.

If the channel is empty, this method waits until there is a message.

If the channel is closed, this method receives a message or returns an error if there are no more messages.

```
use async_channel::{unbounded, RecvError};
let (s, r) = unbounded();
assert_eq!(s.send(1).await, Ok(()));
drop(s);
assert_eq!(r.recv().await, Ok(1));
assert_eq!(r.recv().await, Err(RecvError));
```
[source](https://docs.rs/src/async_channel/lib.rs.html#577-579)#### pub fn [recv_blocking](https://docs.rs#method.recv_blocking)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T, [RecvError](https://docs.rs/struct.RecvError.html)>

[source](https://docs.rs/src/async_channel/lib.rs.html#577-579)

#### pub fn [recv_blocking](https://docs.rs#method.recv_blocking)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T, [RecvError](https://docs.rs/struct.RecvError.html)>

Receives a message from the channel using the blocking strategy.

If the channel is empty, this method waits until there is a message. If the channel is closed, this method receives a message or returns an error if there are no more messages.

Rather than using asynchronous waiting, like the [ recv](https://docs.rs/struct.Receiver.html#method.recv) method,
this method will block the current thread until the message is sent.

This method should not be used in an asynchronous context. It is intended to be used such that a channel can be used in both asynchronous and synchronous contexts. Calling this method in an asynchronous context may result in deadlocks.

```
use async_channel::{unbounded, RecvError};
let (s, r) = unbounded();
assert_eq!(s.send_blocking(1), Ok(()));

assert_eq!(r.recv_blocking(), Ok(1));
assert_eq!(r.recv_blocking(), Err(RecvError));
```

The remaining messages can still be received.

```

# async-global-executor 2.4.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/async-global-executor/2.4.1

# async-global-executor

A global executor built on top of async-executor and async-io

# Features

- `async-io`: if enabled,- `async-global-executor`will use- `async_io::block_on`instead of- `futures_lite::future::block_on`internally. this is preferred if your application also uses- `async-io`.
- `blocking`: enable the use of the- `blocking`crate through- `async_global_executor::spawn_blocking`.
- `tokio`: if enabled,- `async-global-executor`will ensure that all tasks that you will spawn run in the context of a tokio 1.0 runtime, spawning a new one if required.
- `tokio03`: if enabled,- `async-global-executor`will ensure that all tasks that you will spawn run in the context of a tokio 0.3 runtime, spawning a new one if required.
- `tokio02`: if enabled,- `async-global-executor`will ensure that all tasks that you will spawn run in the context of a tokio 0.2 runtime, spawning a new one if required.

# Examples

```
# use futures_lite::future;
// spawn a task on the multi-threaded executor
let task1 = async_global_executor::spawn(async {
    1 + 2
});
// spawn a task on the local executor (same thread)
let task2 = async_global_executor::spawn_local(async {
    3 + 4
});
let task = future::zip(task1, task2);
// run the executor
async_global_executor::block_on(async {
    assert_eq!(task.await, (3, 7));
});
```

at your option.

# async_channel - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/async-channel/^2.1.1/

## Expand description

An async multi-producer multi-consumer channel, where each message can be received by only one of all existing consumers.

There are two kinds of channels:

A channel has the [ Sender](https://docs.rs/struct.Sender.html) and

[side. Both sides are cloneable and can be shared among multiple threads.](https://docs.rs/struct.Receiver.html)

`Receiver`When all [ Sender](https://docs.rs/struct.Sender.html)s or all

[s are dropped, the channel becomes closed. When a channel is closed, no more messages can be sent, but remaining messages can still be received.](https://docs.rs/struct.Receiver.html)

`Receiver`The channel can also be closed manually by calling [ Sender::close()](https://docs.rs/struct.Sender.html#method.close) or

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Receiver.html#method.close)

`Receiver::close()`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
let (s, r) = async_channel::unbounded();
assert_eq!(s.send("Hello").await, Ok(()));
assert_eq!(r.recv().await, Ok("Hello"));
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Closed](https://docs.rs/struct.Closed.html)
- A future returned by `Sender::closed()`
- [Receiver](https://docs.rs/struct.Receiver.html)
- The receiving side of a channel.
- [Recv](https://docs.rs/struct.Recv.html)
- A future returned by `Receiver::recv()`
- [Recv](https://docs.rs/struct.RecvError.html)- Error
- An error returned from `Receiver::recv()`
- [Send](https://docs.rs/struct.Send.html)
- A future returned by `Sender::send()`
- [Send](https://docs.rs/struct.SendError.html)- Error
- An error returned from `Sender::send()`
- [Sender](https://docs.rs/struct.Sender.html)
- The sending side of a channel.
- [Weak](https://docs.rs/struct.WeakReceiver.html)- Receiver
- A `Receiver`
- [Weak](https://docs.rs/struct.WeakSender.html)- Sender
- A `Sender`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [TryRecv](https://docs.rs/enum.TryRecvError.html)- Error
- An error returned from `Receiver::try_recv()`
- [TrySend](https://docs.rs/enum.TrySendError.html)- Error
- An error returned from `Sender::try_send()`

# async_executor - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/async-executor/^1.8/

## Expand description

Async executors.

This crate provides two reference executors that trade performance for
functionality. They should be considered reference executors that are “good
enough” for most use cases. For more specialized use cases, consider writing
your own executor on top of [ async-task](https://crates.io/crates/async-task).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use async_executor::Executor;
use futures_lite::future;
// Create a new executor.
let ex = Executor::new();
// Spawn a task.
let task = ex.spawn(async {
    println!("Hello world");
});
// Run the executor until the task completes.
future::block_on(ex.run(task));
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use async_task::`- [FallibleTask](https://docs.rs/async-task/4.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/async_task/task/struct.FallibleTask.html);
- `pub use async_task::`- [Task](https://docs.rs/async-task/4.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/async_task/task/struct.Task.html);

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Executor](https://docs.rs/struct.Executor.html)
- An async executor.
- [Local](https://docs.rs/struct.LocalExecutor.html)- Executor
- A thread-local executor.
- [Static](https://docs.rs/struct.StaticExecutor.html)- Executor - `static`
- A static-lifetimed async `Executor`
- [Static](https://docs.rs/struct.StaticLocalExecutor.html)- Local - Executor - `static`
- A static async `LocalExecutor``LocalExecutor::leak`

# async_io - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/async-io/^2.2.1/

## Expand description

Async I/O and timers.

This crate provides two tools:

- `Async`- [many other](https://github.com/smol-rs/async-io/tree/master/examples)types) to use in async programs.
- `Timer`

For concrete async networking types built on top of this crate, see [ async-net](https://docs.rs/async-net).

[§](https://docs.rs#implementation)Implementation

The first time [ Async](https://docs.rs/struct.Async.html) or

[is used, a thread named “async-io” will be spawned. The purpose of this thread is to wait for I/O events reported by the operating system, and then wake appropriate futures blocked on I/O or timers when they can be resumed.](https://docs.rs/struct.Timer.html)

`Timer`To wait for the next I/O event, the “async-io” thread uses [epoll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epoll) on Linux/Android/illumos,
[kqueue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kqueue) on macOS/iOS/BSD, [event ports](https://illumos.org/man/port_create) on illumos/Solaris, and [IOCP](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/i-o-completion-ports) on Windows. That
functionality is provided by the [ polling](https://docs.rs/polling) crate.

However, note that you can also process I/O events and wake futures on any thread using the
[ block_on()](https://docs.rs/fn.block_on.html) function. The “async-io” thread is therefore just a fallback mechanism
processing I/O events in case no other threads are.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Connect to `example.com:80`, or time out after 10 seconds.

```
use async_io::{Async, Timer};
use futures_lite::{future::FutureExt, io};
use std::net::{TcpStream, ToSocketAddrs};
use std::time::Duration;
let addr = "example.com:80".to_socket_addrs()?.next().unwrap();
let stream = Async::<TcpStream>::connect(addr).or(async {
    Timer::after(Duration::from_secs(10)).await;
    Err(io::ErrorKind::TimedOut.into())
})
.await?;
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [os](https://docs.rs/os/index.html)
- Platform-specific functionality.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Async](https://docs.rs/struct.Async.html)
- Async adapter for I/O types.
- [Readable](https://docs.rs/struct.Readable.html)
- Future for `Async::readable`
- [Readable](https://docs.rs/struct.ReadableOwned.html)- Owned
- Future for `Async::readable_owned`
- [Timer](https://docs.rs/struct.Timer.html)
- A future or stream that emits timed events.
- [Writable](https://docs.rs/struct.Writable.html)
- Future for `Async::writable`
- [Writable](https://docs.rs/struct.WritableOwned.html)- Owned
- Future for `Async::writable_owned`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [IoSafe](https://docs.rs/trait.IoSafe.html)
- Types whose I/O trait implementations do not drop the underlying I/O source.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [block_](https://docs.rs/fn.block_on.html)- on
- Blocks the current thread on a future, processing I/O events when idle.

# async_lock - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/async-lock/^3.2/

## Expand description

Async synchronization primitives.

This crate provides the following primitives:

- `Barrier`
- `Mutex`
- `RwLock`
- `Semaphore`

[§](https://docs.rs#relationship-with-stdsync)Relationship with `std::sync`

In general, you should consider using [ std::sync](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/index.html) types over types from this crate.

There are two primary use cases for types from this crate:

- You need to use a synchronization primitive in a `no_std`environment.
- You need to hold a lock across an `.await`point. (Holding an`std::sync``.await`will make your future non-`Send`, and is also highly likely to cause deadlocks.)

If you already use `libstd` and you aren’t holding locks across await points (there is a
Clippy lint called [ await_holding_lock](https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-clippy/stable/index.html#/await_holding_lock) that emits warnings for this scenario), you should
consider

[instead of this crate. Those types are optimized for the currently running operating system, are less complex and are generally much faster.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/index.html)

`std::sync`In contrast, `async-lock`’s notification system uses `std::sync::Mutex` under the hood if
the `std` feature is enabled, and will fall back to a significantly slower strategy if it is
not. So, there are few cases where `async-lock` is a win for performance over [ std::sync](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/index.html).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [futures](https://docs.rs/futures/index.html)
- Named futures for use with `async_lock`primitives.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Barrier](https://docs.rs/struct.Barrier.html)
- A counter to synchronize multiple tasks at the same time.
- [Barrier](https://docs.rs/struct.BarrierWaitResult.html)- Wait - Result
- Returned by `Barrier::wait()`
- [Mutex](https://docs.rs/struct.Mutex.html)
- An async mutex.
- [Mutex](https://docs.rs/struct.MutexGuard.html)- Guard
- A guard that releases the mutex when dropped.
- [Mutex](https://docs.rs/struct.MutexGuardArc.html)- Guard - Arc
- An owned guard that releases the mutex when dropped.
- [Once](https://docs.rs/struct.OnceCell.html)- Cell
- A memory location that can be written to at most once.
- [RwLock](https://docs.rs/struct.RwLock.html)
- An async reader-writer lock.
- [RwLock](https://docs.rs/struct.RwLockReadGuard.html)- Read - Guard
- A guard that releases the read lock when dropped.
- [RwLock](https://docs.rs/struct.RwLockReadGuardArc.html)- Read - Guard - Arc
- An owned, reference-counting guard that releases the read lock when dropped.
- [RwLock](https://docs.rs/struct.RwLockUpgradableReadGuard.html)- Upgradable - Read - Guard
- A guard that releases the upgradable read lock when dropped.
- [RwLock](https://docs.rs/struct.RwLockUpgradableReadGuardArc.html)- Upgradable - Read - Guard - Arc
- An owned, reference-counting guard that releases the upgradable read lock when dropped.
- [RwLock](https://docs.rs/struct.RwLockWriteGuard.html)- Write - Guard
- A guard that releases the write lock when dropped.
- [RwLock](https://docs.rs/struct.RwLockWriteGuardArc.html)- Write - Guard - Arc
- An owned, reference-counted guard that releases the write lock when dropped.
- [Semaphore](https://docs.rs/struct.Semaphore.html)
- A counter for limiting the number of concurrent operations.
- [Semaphore](https://docs.rs/struct.SemaphoreGuard.html)- Guard
- A guard that releases the acquired permit.
- [Semaphore](https://docs.rs/struct.SemaphoreGuardArc.html)- Guard - Arc
- An owned guard that releases the acquired permit.

---

# blocking - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/blocking/^1.5/

## Expand description

A thread pool for isolating blocking I/O in async programs.

Sometimes there’s no way to avoid blocking I/O. Consider files or stdin, which have weak async
support on modern operating systems. While [IOCP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Input/output_completion_port), [AIO](http://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/io_submit.2.html), and [io_uring](https://lwn.net/Articles/776703) are possible
solutions, they’re not always available or ideal.

Since blocking is not allowed inside futures, we must move blocking I/O onto a special thread pool provided by this crate. The pool dynamically spawns and stops threads depending on the current number of running I/O jobs.

Note that there is a limit on the number of active threads. Once that limit is hit, a running job has to finish before others get a chance to run. When a thread is idle, it waits for the next job or shuts down after a certain timeout.

The default number of threads (set to 500) can be altered by setting BLOCKING_MAX_THREADS environment variable with value between 1 and 10000.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Read the contents of a file:

```
use blocking::unblock;
use std::fs;
let contents = unblock(|| fs::read_to_string("file.txt")).await?;
println!("{}", contents);
```
Read a file and pipe its contents to stdout:

```
use blocking::{unblock, Unblock};
use futures_lite::io;
use std::fs::File;
let input = unblock(|| File::open("file.txt")).await?;
let input = Unblock::new(input);
let mut output = Unblock::new(std::io::stdout());
io::copy(input, &mut output).await?;
```
Iterate over the contents of a directory:

```
use blocking::Unblock;
use futures_lite::prelude::*;
use std::fs;
let mut dir = Unblock::new(fs::read_dir(".")?);
while let Some(item) = dir.next().await {
    println!("{}", item?.file_name().to_string_lossy());
}
```
Spawn a process:

```
use blocking::unblock;
use std::process::Command;
let out = unblock(|| Command::new("dir").output()).await?;
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use async_task::`- [Task](https://docs.rs/async-task/4.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/async_task/task/struct.Task.html);

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Unblock](https://docs.rs/struct.Unblock.html)
- Runs blocking I/O on a thread pool.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [unblock](https://docs.rs/fn.unblock.html)
- Runs blocking code on a thread pool.

# futures_lite - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/futures-lite/^2.0/

## Expand description

Futures, streams, and async I/O combinators.

This crate is a subset of [futures](https://docs.rs/futures) that compiles an order of magnitude faster, fixes minor
warts in its API, fills in some obvious gaps, and removes almost all unsafe code from it.

In short, this crate aims to be more enjoyable than [futures](https://docs.rs/futures) but still fully compatible with
it.

The API for this crate is intentionally constrained. Please consult the [features list](https://github.com/smol-rs/futures-lite/blob/master/FEATURES.md) for
APIs that are occluded from this crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use futures_lite::future;
fn main() {
    future::block_on(async {
        println!("Hello world!");
    })
}
```

# once_cell - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/once_cell/^1.4/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

`once_cell` provides two new cell-like types, [ unsync::OnceCell](https://docs.rs/unsync/struct.OnceCell.html) and

[. A](https://docs.rs/sync/struct.OnceCell.html)

`sync::OnceCell``OnceCell` might store arbitrary non-`Copy` types, can
be assigned to at most once and provides direct access to the stored
contents. The core API looks *roughly*like this (and there’s much more inside, read on!):

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
impl<T> OnceCell<T> {
    const fn new() -> OnceCell<T> { ... }
    fn set(&self, value: T) -> Result<(), T> { ... }
    fn get(&self) -> Option<&T> { ... }
}
```
Note that, like with [ RefCell](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/cell/struct.RefCell.html) and

[, the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Mutex.html)

`Mutex``set` method requires
only a shared reference. Because of the single assignment restriction `get`
can return a `&T` instead of `Ref<T>` or `MutexGuard<T>`.The `sync` flavor is thread-safe (that is, implements the [ Sync](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/marker/trait.Sync.html) trait),
while the

`unsync` one is not.[§](https://docs.rs#recipes)Recipes

`OnceCell` might be useful for a variety of patterns.

[§](https://docs.rs#safe-initialization-of-global-data)Safe Initialization of Global Data

```
use std::{env, io};
use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct Logger {
    // ...
}
static INSTANCE: OnceCell<Logger> = OnceCell::new();
impl Logger {
    pub fn global() -> &'static Logger {
        INSTANCE.get().expect("logger is not initialized")
    }
    fn from_cli(args: env::Args) -> Result<Logger, std::io::Error> {
       // ...
    }
}
fn main() {
    let logger = Logger::from_cli(env::args()).unwrap();
    INSTANCE.set(logger).unwrap();
    // use `Logger::global()` from now on
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#lazy-initialized-global-data)Lazy Initialized Global Data

This is essentially the `lazy_static!` macro, but without a macro.

```
use std::{sync::Mutex, collections::HashMap};
use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
fn global_data() -> &'static Mutex<HashMap<i32, String>> {
    static INSTANCE: OnceCell<Mutex<HashMap<i32, String>>> = OnceCell::new();
    INSTANCE.get_or_init(|| {
        let mut m = HashMap::new();
        m.insert(13, "Spica".to_string());
        m.insert(74, "Hoyten".to_string());
        Mutex::new(m)
    })
}
```
There are also the [ sync::Lazy](https://docs.rs/sync/struct.Lazy.html) and

[convenience types to streamline this pattern:](https://docs.rs/unsync/struct.Lazy.html)

`unsync::Lazy````
use std::{sync::Mutex, collections::HashMap};
use once_cell::sync::Lazy;
static GLOBAL_DATA: Lazy<Mutex<HashMap<i32, String>>> = Lazy::new(|| {
    let mut m = HashMap::new();
    m.insert(13, "Spica".to_string());
    m.insert(74, "Hoyten".to_string());
    Mutex::new(m)
});
fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", GLOBAL_DATA.lock().unwrap());
}
```
Note that the variable that holds `Lazy` is declared as `static`, *not*
`const`. This is important: using `const` instead compiles, but works wrong.

[§](https://docs.rs#general-purpose-lazy-evaluation)General purpose lazy evaluation

Unlike `lazy_static!`, `Lazy` works with local variables.

```
use once_cell::unsync::Lazy;
fn main() {
    let ctx = vec![1, 2, 3];
    let thunk = Lazy::new(|| {
        ctx.iter().sum::<i32>()
    });
    assert_eq!(*thunk, 6);
}
```
If you need a lazy field in a struct, you probably should use `OnceCell`
directly, because that will allow you to access `self` during
initialization.

```
use std::{fs, path::PathBuf};
use once_cell::unsync::OnceCell;
struct Ctx {
    config_path: PathBuf,
    config: OnceCell<String>,
}
impl Ctx {
    pub fn get_config(&self) -> Result<&str, std::io::Error> {
        let cfg = self.config.get_or_try_init(|| {
            fs::read_to_string(&self.config_path)
        })?;
        Ok(cfg.as_str())
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#lazily-compiled-regex)Lazily Compiled Regex

This is a `regex!` macro which takes a string literal and returns an
*expression* that evaluates to a `&'static Regex`:

```
macro_rules! regex {
    ($re:literal $(,)?) => {{
        static RE: once_cell::sync::OnceCell<regex::Regex> = once_cell::sync::OnceCell::new();
        RE.get_or_init(|| regex::Regex::new($re).unwrap())
    }};
}
```
This macro can be useful to avoid the “compile regex on every loop iteration” problem.

[§](https://docs.rs#runtime-include_bytes)Runtime `include_bytes!`

The `include_bytes` macro is useful to include test resources, but it slows
down test compilation a lot. An alternative is to load the resources at
runtime:

```
use std::path::Path;
use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
pub struct TestResource {
    path: &'static str,
    cell: OnceCell<Vec<u8>>,
}
impl TestResource {
    pub const fn new(path: &'static str) -> TestResource {
        TestResource { path, cell: OnceCell::new() }
    }
    pub fn bytes(&self) -> &[u8] {
        self.cell.get_or_init(|| {
            let dir = std::env::var("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR").unwrap();
            let path = Path::new(dir.as_str()).join(self.path);
            std::fs::read(&path).unwrap_or_else(|_err| {
                panic!("failed to load test resource: {}", path.display())
            })
        }).as_slice()
    }
}
static TEST_IMAGE: TestResource = TestResource::new("test_data/lena.png");
#[test]
fn test_sobel_filter() {
    let rgb: &[u8] = TEST_IMAGE.bytes();
    // ...
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#lateinit)`lateinit`

`LateInit` type for delayed initialization. It is reminiscent of Kotlin’s
`lateinit` keyword and allows construction of cyclic data structures:

```
use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
pub struct LateInit<T> { cell: OnceCell<T> }
impl<T> LateInit<T> {
    pub fn init(&self, value: T) {
        assert!(self.cell.set(value).is_ok())
    }
}
impl<T> Default for LateInit<T> {
    fn default() -> Self { LateInit { cell: OnceCell::default() } }
}
impl<T> std::ops::Deref for LateInit<T> {
    type Target = T;
    fn deref(&self) -> &T {
        self.cell.get().unwrap()
    }
}
#[derive(Default)]
struct A<'a> {
    b: LateInit<&'a B<'a>>,
}
#[derive(Default)]
struct B<'a> {
    a: LateInit<&'a A<'a>>
}
fn build_cycle() {
    let a = A::default();
    let b = B::default();
    a.b.init(&b);
    b.a.init(&a);
    let _a = &a.b.a.b.a;
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#comparison-with-std)Comparison with std

| `!Sync`types | Access Mode | Drawbacks |
|---|---|---|
| `Cell<T>` | `T` | requires `T: Copy`for`get` |
| `RefCell<T>` | `RefMut<T>`/`Ref<T>` | may panic at runtime |
| `unsync::OnceCell<T>` | `&T` | assignable only once |

| `Sync`types | Access Mode | Drawbacks |
|---|---|---|
| `AtomicT` | `T` | works only with certain `Copy`types |
| `Mutex<T>` | `MutexGuard<T>` | may deadlock at runtime, may block the thread |
| `sync::OnceCell<T>` | `&T` | assignable only once, may block the thread |

Technically, calling `get_or_init` will also cause a panic or a deadlock if
it recursively calls itself. However, because the assignment can happen only
once, such cases should be more rare than equivalents with `RefCell` and
`Mutex`.

[§](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rustc-version)Minimum Supported `rustc` Version

If only the `std`, `alloc`, or `race` features are enabled, MSRV will be
updated conservatively, supporting at least latest 8 versions of the compiler.
When using other features, like `parking_lot`, MSRV might be updated more
frequently, up to the latest stable. In both cases, increasing MSRV is *not*
considered a semver-breaking change and requires only a minor version bump.

[§](https://docs.rs#implementation-details)Implementation details

The implementation is based on the
[ lazy_static](https://github.com/rust-lang-nursery/lazy-static.rs/) and

[crates and](https://github.com/indiv0/lazycell/)

`lazy_cell`[. In some sense,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Once.html)

`std::sync::Once``once_cell` just streamlines and unifies
those APIs.To implement a sync flavor of `OnceCell`, this crates uses either a custom
re-implementation of `std::sync::Once` or `parking_lot::Mutex`. This is
controlled by the `parking_lot` feature (disabled by default). Performance
is the same for both cases, but the `parking_lot` based `OnceCell<T>` is
smaller by up to 16 bytes.

This crate uses `unsafe`.

[§](https://docs.rs#faq)F.A.Q.

**Should I use the sync or unsync flavor?**

Because Rust compiler checks thread safety for you, it’s impossible to
accidentally use `unsync` where `sync` is required. So, use `unsync` in
single-threaded code and `sync` in multi-threaded. It’s easy to switch
between the two if code becomes multi-threaded later.

At the moment, `unsync` has an additional benefit that reentrant
initialization causes a panic, which might be easier to debug than a
deadlock.

**Does this crate support async?**

No, but you can use
[ async_once_cell](https://crates.io/crates/async_once_cell) instead.

**Does this crate support  no_std?**

Yes, but with caveats. `OnceCell` is a synchronization primitive which
*semantically* relies on blocking. `OnceCell` guarantees that at most one
`f` will be called to compute the value. If two threads of execution call
`get_or_init` concurrently, one of them has to wait.

Waiting fundamentally requires OS support. Execution environment needs to
understand who waits on whom to prevent deadlocks due to priority inversion.
You *could* make code to compile by blindly using pure spinlocks, but the
runtime behavior would be subtly wrong.

Given these constraints, `once_cell` provides the following options:

- The `race`module provides similar, but distinct synchronization primitive which is compatible with`no_std`. With`race`, the`f`function can be called multiple times by different threads, but only one thread will win to install the value.
- `critical-section`feature (with a- `-`, not- `_`) uses- `critical_section`to implement blocking.

**Can I bring my own mutex?**

There is [generic_once_cell](https://crates.io/crates/generic_once_cell) to
allow just that.

**Should I use  std::cell::OnceCell, once_cell, or lazy_static?**

If you can use `std` version (your MSRV is at least 1.70, and you don’t need
extra features `once_cell` provides), use `std`. Otherwise, use `once_cell`.
Don’t use `lazy_static`.

[§](https://docs.rs#related-crates)Related crates

- Most of this crate’s functionality is available in `std`starting with Rust 1.70. See`std::cell::OnceCell`and`std::sync::OnceLock`.
- [double-checked-cell](https://github.com/niklasf/double-checked-cell)
- [lazy-init](https://crates.io/crates/lazy-init)
- [lazycell](https://crates.io/crates/lazycell)
- [mitochondria](https://crates.io/crates/mitochondria)
- [lazy_static](https://crates.io/crates/lazy_static)
- [async_once_cell](https://crates.io/crates/async_once_cell)
- [generic_once_cell](https://crates.io/crates/generic_once_cell)(bring your own mutex)

---

# tokio - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tokio/^1.0/

## Expand description

A runtime for writing reliable network applications without compromising speed.

Tokio is an event-driven, non-blocking I/O platform for writing asynchronous applications with the Rust programming language. At a high level, it provides a few major components:

- Tools for [working with asynchronous tasks](https://docs.rs#working-with-tasks), including[synchronization primitives and channels](https://docs.rs/sync/index.html)and[timeouts, sleeps, and intervals](https://docs.rs/time/index.html).
- APIs for [performing asynchronous I/O](https://docs.rs#asynchronous-io), including[TCP and UDP](https://docs.rs/net/index.html)sockets,[filesystem](https://docs.rs/fs/index.html)operations, and[process](https://docs.rs/process/index.html)and[signal](https://docs.rs/signal/index.html)management.
- A [runtime](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html)for executing asynchronous code, including a task scheduler, an I/O driver backed by the operating system’s event queue (`epoll`,`kqueue`,`IOCP`, etc…), and a high performance timer.

Guide level documentation is found on the [website](https://tokio.rs/tokio/tutorial).

[§](https://docs.rs#a-tour-of-tokio)A Tour of Tokio

Tokio consists of a number of modules that provide a range of functionality essential for implementing asynchronous applications in Rust. In this section, we will take a brief tour of Tokio, summarizing the major APIs and their uses.

The easiest way to get started is to enable all features. Do this by
enabling the `full` feature flag:

`tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }`[§](https://docs.rs#authoring-applications)Authoring applications

Tokio is great for writing applications and most users in this case shouldn’t
worry too much about what features they should pick. If you’re unsure, we suggest
going with `full` to ensure that you don’t run into any road blocks while you’re
building your application.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

This example shows the quickest way to get started with Tokio.

`tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }`[§](https://docs.rs#authoring-libraries)Authoring libraries

As a library author your goal should be to provide the lightest weight crate that is based on Tokio. To achieve this you should ensure that you only enable the features you need. This allows users to pick up your crate without having to enable unnecessary features.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

This example shows how you may want to import features for a library that just
needs to `tokio::spawn` and use a `TcpStream`.

`tokio = { version = "1", features = ["rt", "net"] }`[§](https://docs.rs#working-with-tasks)Working With Tasks

Asynchronous programs in Rust are based around lightweight, non-blocking
units of execution called [ tasks](https://docs.rs#working-with-tasks). The

[module provides important tools for working with tasks:](https://docs.rs/task/index.html)

`tokio::task`- The `spawn``JoinHandle`
- Functions for [running blocking operations](https://docs.rs/task/index.html#blocking-and-yielding)in an asynchronous task context.

The [ tokio::task](https://docs.rs/task/index.html) module is present only when the “rt” feature flag
is enabled.

The [ tokio::sync](https://docs.rs/sync/index.html) module contains synchronization primitives to use when
needing to communicate or share data. These include:

- channels (`oneshot``mpsc``watch``broadcast`
- a non-blocking `Mutex`
- an asynchronous `Barrier`

The `tokio::sync` module is present only when the “sync” feature flag is
enabled.

The [ tokio::time](https://docs.rs/time/index.html) module provides utilities for tracking time and
scheduling work. This includes functions for setting

[timeouts](https://docs.rs/time/fn.timeout.html)for tasks,

[sleeping](https://docs.rs/time/fn.sleep.html)work to run in the future, or

[repeating an operation at an interval](https://docs.rs/time/fn.interval.html).

In order to use `tokio::time`, the “time” feature flag must be enabled.

Finally, Tokio provides a *runtime* for executing asynchronous tasks. Most
applications can use the [ #[tokio::main]](https://docs.rs/attr.main.html) macro to run their code on the
Tokio runtime. However, this macro provides only basic configuration options. As
an alternative, the

[module provides more powerful APIs for configuring and managing runtimes. You should use that module if the](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html)

`tokio::runtime``#[tokio::main]` macro doesn’t
provide the functionality you need.Using the runtime requires the “rt” or “rt-multi-thread” feature flags, to
enable the current-thread [single-threaded scheduler](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html#current-thread-scheduler) and the [multi-thread
scheduler](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html#multi-thread-scheduler), respectively. See the [ runtime module
documentation](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html#runtime-scheduler) for details. In addition, the “macros” feature
flag enables the

`#[tokio::main]` and `#[tokio::test]` attributes.[§](https://docs.rs#cpu-bound-tasks-and-blocking-code)CPU-bound tasks and blocking code

Tokio is able to concurrently run many tasks on a few threads by repeatedly
swapping the currently running task on each thread. However, this kind of
swapping can only happen at `.await` points, so code that spends a long time
without reaching an `.await` will prevent other tasks from running. To
combat this, Tokio provides two kinds of threads: Core threads and blocking threads.

The core threads are where all asynchronous code runs, and Tokio will by default
spawn one for each CPU core. You can use the environment variable `TOKIO_WORKER_THREADS`
to override the default value.

The blocking threads are spawned on demand, can be used to run blocking code
that would otherwise block other tasks from running and are kept alive when
not used for a certain amount of time which can be configured with [ thread_keep_alive](https://docs.rs/runtime/struct.Builder.html#method.thread_keep_alive).
Since it is not possible for Tokio to swap out blocking tasks, like it
can do with asynchronous code, the upper limit on the number of blocking
threads is very large. These limits can be configured on the

[.](https://docs.rs/runtime/struct.Builder.html)

`Builder`To spawn a blocking task, you should use the [ spawn_blocking](https://docs.rs/task/fn.spawn_blocking.html) function.

```
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    // This is running on a core thread.
    let blocking_task = tokio::task::spawn_blocking(|| {
        // This is running on a blocking thread.
        // Blocking here is ok.
    });
    // We can wait for the blocking task like this:
    // If the blocking task panics, the unwrap below will propagate the
    // panic.
    blocking_task.await.unwrap();
}
```
If your code is CPU-bound and you wish to limit the number of threads used
to run it, you should use a separate thread pool dedicated to CPU bound tasks.
For example, you could consider using the [rayon](https://docs.rs/rayon) library for CPU-bound
tasks. It is also possible to create an extra Tokio runtime dedicated to
CPU-bound tasks, but if you do this, you should be careful that the extra
runtime runs *only* CPU-bound tasks, as IO-bound tasks on that runtime
will behave poorly.

Hint: If using rayon, you can use a [ oneshot](https://docs.rs/sync/oneshot/index.html) channel to send the result back
to Tokio when the rayon task finishes.

[§](https://docs.rs#asynchronous-io)Asynchronous IO

As well as scheduling and running tasks, Tokio provides everything you need to perform input and output asynchronously.

The [ tokio::io](https://docs.rs/io/index.html) module provides Tokio’s asynchronous core I/O primitives,
the

[,](https://docs.rs/io/trait.AsyncRead.html)

`AsyncRead`[, and](https://docs.rs/io/trait.AsyncWrite.html)

`AsyncWrite`[traits. In addition, when the “io-util” feature flag is enabled, it also provides combinators and functions for working with these traits, forming as an asynchronous counterpart to](https://docs.rs/io/trait.AsyncBufRead.html)

`AsyncBufRead`[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/index.html)

`std::io`Tokio also includes APIs for performing various kinds of I/O and interacting with the operating system asynchronously. These include:

- `tokio::net`- [TCP](https://docs.rs/net/tcp/index.html),- [UDP](https://docs.rs/net/struct.UdpSocket.html), and- [Unix Domain Sockets](https://docs.rs/net/unix/index.html)(enabled by the “net” feature flag),
- `tokio::fs`- `std::fs`
- `tokio::signal`
- `tokio::process`

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

A simple TCP echo server:

```
use tokio::net::TcpListener;
use tokio::io::{AsyncReadExt, AsyncWriteExt};
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let listener = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:8080").await?;
    loop {
        let (mut socket, _) = listener.accept().await?;
        tokio::spawn(async move {
            let mut buf = [0; 1024];
            // In a loop, read data from the socket and write the data back.
            loop {
                let n = match socket.read(&mut buf).await {
                    // socket closed
                    Ok(0) => return,
                    Ok(n) => n,
                    Err(e) => {
                        eprintln!("failed to read from socket; err = {:?}", e);
                        return;
                    }
                };
                // Write the data back
                if let Err(e) = socket.write_all(&buf[0..n]).await {
                    eprintln!("failed to write to socket; err = {:?}", e);
                    return;
                }
            }
        });
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature flags

Tokio uses a set of [feature flags](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-features-section) to reduce the amount of compiled code. It
is possible to just enable certain features over others. By default, Tokio
does not enable any features but allows one to enable a subset for their use
case. Below is a list of the available feature flags. You may also notice
above each function, struct and trait there is listed one or more feature flags
that are required for that item to be used. If you are new to Tokio it is
recommended that you use the `full` feature flag which will enable all public APIs.
Beware though that this will pull in many extra dependencies that you may not
need.

- `full`: Enables all features listed below except- `test-util`and unstable features.
- `rt`: Enables- `tokio::spawn`, the current-thread scheduler, and non-scheduler utilities.
- `rt-multi-thread`: Enables the heavier, multi-threaded, work-stealing scheduler.
- `io-util`: Enables the IO based- `Ext`traits.
- `io-std`: Enable- `Stdout`,- `Stdin`and- `Stderr`types.
- `net`: Enables- `tokio::net`types such as- `TcpStream`,- `UnixStream`and- `UdpSocket`, as well as (on Unix-like systems)- `AsyncFd`and (on FreeBSD)- `PollAio`.
- `time`: Enables- `tokio::time`types and allows the schedulers to enable the built-in timer.
- `process`: Enables- `tokio::process`types.
- `macros`: Enables- `#[tokio::main]`and- `#[tokio::test]`macros.
- `sync`: Enables all- `tokio::sync`types.
- `signal`: Enables all- `tokio::signal`types.
- `fs`: Enables- `tokio::fs`types.
- `test-util`: Enables testing based infrastructure for the Tokio runtime.
- `parking_lot`: As a potential optimization, use the- `parking_lot`- `const`context.- `MSRV`may increase according to the- `parking_lot`

*Note:  AsyncRead and AsyncWrite traits do not require any features and are
always available.*

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-features)Unstable features

Some feature flags are only available when specifying the `tokio_unstable` flag:

- `tracing`: Enables tracing events.
- `io-uring`: Enables- `io-uring`(Linux only).
- `taskdump`: Enables- `taskdump`(Linux only).

Likewise, this flag enables access to unstable APIs.

This flag enables **unstable** features. The public API of these features
may break in 1.x releases. To enable these features, the `--cfg tokio_unstable` argument must be passed to `rustc` when compiling. This
serves to explicitly opt-in to features which may break semver conventions,
since Cargo [does not yet directly support such opt-ins](https://internals.rust-lang.org/t/feature-request-unstable-opt-in-non-transitive-crate-features/16193#why-not-a-crate-feature-2).

You can specify it in your project’s `.cargo/config.toml` file:

```
[build]
rustflags = ["--cfg", "tokio_unstable"]
```
`[build]` section does **not**go in a

`Cargo.toml` file. Instead it must be placed in the Cargo config
file `.cargo/config.toml`.
Alternatively, you can specify it with an environment variable:

```
## Many *nix shells:
export RUSTFLAGS="--cfg tokio_unstable"
cargo build
```
```
## Windows PowerShell:
$Env:RUSTFLAGS="--cfg tokio_unstable"
cargo build
```
[§](https://docs.rs#supported-platforms)Supported platforms

Tokio currently guarantees support for the following platforms:

- Linux
- Windows
- Android (API level 21)
- macOS
- iOS
- FreeBSD

Tokio will continue to support these platforms in the future. However, future releases may change requirements such as the minimum required libc version on Linux, the API level on Android, or the supported FreeBSD release.

Beyond the above platforms, Tokio is intended to work on all platforms
supported by the mio crate. You can find a longer list [in mio’s
documentation](https://crates.io/crates/mio#platforms). However, these additional platforms may
become unsupported in the future.

Note that Wine is considered to be a different platform from Windows. See mio’s documentation for more information on Wine support.

[§](https://docs.rs#wasm-support)`WASM` support

Tokio has some limited support for the `WASM` platform. Without the
`tokio_unstable` flag, the following features are supported:

- `sync`
- `macros`
- `io-util`
- `rt`
- `time`

Enabling any other feature (including `full`) will cause a compilation
failure.

The `time` module will only work on `WASM` platforms that have support for
timers (e.g. wasm32-wasi). The timing functions will panic if used on a `WASM`
platform that does not support timers.

Note also that if the runtime becomes indefinitely idle, it will panic immediately instead of blocking forever. On platforms that don’t support time, this means that the runtime can never be idle in any way.

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-wasm-support)Unstable `WASM` support

Tokio also has unstable support for some additional `WASM` features. This
requires the use of the `tokio_unstable` flag.

Using this flag enables the use of `tokio::net` on the wasm32-wasi target.
However, not all methods are available on the networking types as `WASI`
currently does not support the creation of new sockets from within `WASM`.
Because of this, sockets must currently be created via the `FromRawFd`
trait.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use task::`- [spawn](https://docs.rs/task/fn.spawn.html);- `rt`

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [doc](https://docs.rs/doc/index.html)- `docsrs`and Unix
- Types which are documented locally in the Tokio crate, but does not actually live here.
- [fs](https://docs.rs/fs/index.html)- `fs`
- Asynchronous file utilities.
- [io](https://docs.rs/io/index.html)
- Traits, helpers, and type definitions for asynchronous I/O functionality.
- [net](https://docs.rs/net/index.html)
- TCP/UDP/Unix bindings for `tokio`.
- [process](https://docs.rs/process/index.html)- `process`
- An implementation of asynchronous process management for Tokio.
- [runtime](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html)- `rt`
- The Tokio runtime.
- [signal](https://docs.rs/signal/index.html)- `signal`
- Asynchronous signal handling for Tokio.
- [stream](https://docs.rs/stream/index.html)
- Due to the `Stream`trait’s inclusion in`std`landing later than Tokio’s 1.0 release, most of the Tokio stream utilities have been moved into the`tokio-stream`
- [sync](https://docs.rs/sync/index.html)- `sync`
- Synchronization primitives for use in asynchronous contexts.
- [task](https://docs.rs/task/index.html)- `rt`
- Asynchronous green-threads.
- [time](https://docs.rs/time/index.html)- `time`
- Utilities for tracking time.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [join](https://docs.rs/macro.join.html)- `macros`
- Waits on multiple concurrent branches, returning when **all**branches complete.
- [pin](https://docs.rs/macro.pin.html)
- Pins a value on the stack.
- [select](https://docs.rs/macro.select.html)- `macros`
- Waits on multiple concurrent branches, returning when the **first**branch completes, cancelling the remaining branches.
- [task_](https://docs.rs/macro.task_local.html)- local - `rt`
- Declares a new task-local key of type `tokio::task::LocalKey`
- [try_](https://docs.rs/macro.try_join.html)- join - `macros`
- Waits on multiple concurrent branches, returning when **all**branches complete with`Ok(_)`or on the first`Err(_)`.

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [main](https://docs.rs/attr.main.html)- `rt`and- `macros`
- Marks async function to be executed by the selected runtime. This macro
helps set up a `Runtime`without requiring the user to use[Runtime](https://docs.rs/tokio/runtime/struct.Runtime.html)or[Builder](https://docs.rs/tokio/runtime/struct.Builder.html)directly.
- [test](https://docs.rs/attr.test.html)- `rt`and- `macros`
- Marks async function to be executed by runtime, suitable to test environment.
This macro helps set up a `Runtime`without requiring the user to use[Runtime](https://docs.rs/tokio/runtime/struct.Runtime.html)or[Builder](https://docs.rs/tokio/runtime/struct.Builder.html)directly.

# tokio - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tokio/^0.2/

A runtime for writing reliable, asynchronous, and slim applications.

Tokio is an event-driven, non-blocking I/O platform for writing asynchronous applications with the Rust programming language. At a high level, it provides a few major components:

- Tools for [working with asynchronous tasks](https://docs.rs#working-with-tasks), including[synchronization primitives and channels](https://docs.rs/tokio/sync/index.html)and[timeouts, delays, and intervals](https://docs.rs/tokio/time/index.html).
- APIs for [performing asynchronous I/O](https://docs.rs#asynchronous-io), including[TCP and UDP](https://docs.rs/tokio/net/index.html)sockets,[filesystem](https://docs.rs/tokio/fs/index.html)operations, and[process](https://docs.rs/tokio/process/index.html)and[signal](https://docs.rs/tokio/signal/index.html)management.
- A [runtime](https://docs.rs/tokio/runtime/index.html)for executing asynchronous code, including a task scheduler, an I/O driver backed by the operating system's event queue (epoll, kqueue, IOCP, etc...), and a high performance timer.

Guide level documentation is found on the [website](https://tokio.rs/tokio/tutorial).

Tokio consists of a number of modules that provide a range of functionality essential for implementing asynchronous applications in Rust. In this section, we will take a brief tour of Tokio, summarizing the major APIs and their uses.

The easiest way to get started is to enable all features. Do this by
enabling the `full` feature flag:

```
tokio = { version = "0.2", features = ["full"] }
```
Tokio uses a set of [feature flags](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-features-section) to reduce the amount of compiled code. It
is possible to just enable certain features over others. By default, Tokio
does not enable any features but allows one to enable a subset for their use
case. Below is a list of the available feature flags. You may also notice
above each function, struct and trait there is listed one or more feature flags
that are required for that item to be used. If you are new to Tokio it is
recommended that you use the `full` feature flag which will enable all public APIs.
Beware though that this will pull in many extra dependencies that you may not
need.

- `full`: Enables all Tokio public API features listed below.
- `rt-core`: Enables- `tokio::spawn`and the basic (single-threaded) scheduler.
- `rt-threaded`: Enables the heavier, multi-threaded, work-stealing scheduler.
- `rt-util`: Enables non-scheduler utilities.
- `io-driver`: Enables the- `mio`based IO driver.
- `io-util`: Enables the IO based- `Ext`traits.
- `io-std`: Enable- `Stdout`,- `Stdin`and- `Stderr`types.
- `net`: Enables- `tokio::net`types such as- `TcpStream`,- `UnixStream`and- `UdpSocket`.
- `tcp`: Enables all- `tokio::net::tcp`types.
- `udp`: Enables all- `tokio::net::udp`types.
- `uds`: Enables all- `tokio::net::unix`types.
- `time`: Enables- `tokio::time`types and allows the schedulers to enable the built in timer.
- `process`: Enables- `tokio::process`types.
- `macros`: Enables- `#[tokio::main]`and- `#[tokio::test]`macros.
- `sync`: Enables all- `tokio::sync`types.
- `stream`: Enables optional- `Stream`implementations for types within Tokio.
- `signal`: Enables all- `tokio::signal`types.
- `fs`: Enables- `tokio::fs`types.
- `dns`: Enables async- `tokio::net::ToSocketAddrs`.
- `test-util`: Enables testing based infrastructure for the Tokio runtime.
- `blocking`: Enables- `block_in_place`and- `spawn_blocking`.

*Note:  AsyncRead and AsyncWrite traits do not require any features and are
always available.*

These features do not expose any new API, but influence internal
implementation aspects of Tokio, and can pull in additional
dependencies. They are not included in `full`:

- `parking_lot`: As a potential optimization, use the- *parking_lot*crate's synchronization primitives internally. MSRV may increase according to the- *parking_lot*release in use.

Tokio is great for writing applications and most users in this case shouldn't
worry too much about what features they should pick. If you're unsure, we suggest
going with `full` to ensure that you don't run into any road blocks while you're
building your application.

This example shows the quickest way to get started with Tokio.

```
tokio = { version = "0.2", features = ["full"] }
```
As a library author your goal should be to provide the lighest weight crate that is based on Tokio. To achieve this you should ensure that you only enable the features you need. This allows users to pick up your crate without having to enable unnecessary features.

This example shows how you may want to import features for a library that just
needs to `tokio::spawn` and use a `TcpStream`.

```
tokio = { version = "0.2", features = ["rt-core", "tcp"] }
```
Asynchronous programs in Rust are based around lightweight, non-blocking
units of execution called [ tasks](https://docs.rs#working-with-tasks). The

[module provides important tools for working with tasks:](https://docs.rs/tokio/task/index.html)

`tokio::task`- The `spawn``JoinHandle`
- Functions for [running blocking operations](https://docs.rs/task/index.html#blocking-and-yielding)in an asynchronous task context.

The [ tokio::task](https://docs.rs/tokio/task/index.html) module is present only when the "rt-core" feature flag
is enabled.

The [ tokio::sync](https://docs.rs/tokio/sync/index.html) module contains synchronization primitives to use when
needing to communicate or share data. These include:

- channels (`oneshot``mpsc``watch`
- a non-blocking `Mutex`
- an asynchronous `Barrier`

The `tokio::sync` module is present only when the "sync" feature flag is
enabled.

The [ tokio::time](https://docs.rs/tokio/time/index.html) module provides utilities for tracking time and
scheduling work. This includes functions for setting

[timeouts](https://docs.rs/tokio/time/fn.timeout.html)for tasks,

[delaying](https://docs.rs/tokio/time/fn.delay_for.html)work to run in the future, or

[repeating an operation at an interval](https://docs.rs/tokio/time/fn.interval.html).

In order to use `tokio::time`, the "time" feature flag must be enabled.

Finally, Tokio provides a *runtime* for executing asynchronous tasks. Most
applications can use the [ #[tokio::main]](https://docs.rs/attr.main.html) macro to run their code on the
Tokio runtime. In use-cases where manual control over the runtime is
required, the

[module provides APIs for configuring and managing runtimes.](https://docs.rs/tokio/runtime/index.html)

`tokio::runtime`Using the runtime requires the "rt-core" or "rt-threaded" feature flags, to
enable the basic [single-threaded scheduler](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html#basic-scheduler) and the [thread-pool
scheduler](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html#threaded-scheduler), respectively. See the [ runtime module
documentation](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html#runtime-scheduler) for details. In addition, the "macros" feature
flag enables the

`#[tokio::main]` and `#[tokio::test]` attributes.Tokio is able to concurrently run many tasks on a few threads by repeatedly
swapping the currently running task on each thread. However, this kind of
swapping can only happen at `.await` points, so code that spends a long time
without reaching an `.await` will prevent other tasks from running. To
combat this, Tokio provides two kinds of threads: Core threads and blocking
threads. The core threads are where all asynchronous code runs, and Tokio
will by default spawn one for each CPU core. The blocking threads are
spawned on demand, and can be used to run blocking code that would otherwise
block other tasks from running. Since it is not possible for Tokio to swap
out blocking tasks, like it can do with asynchronous code, the upper limit
on the number of blocking threads is very large. These limits can be
configured on the [ Builder](https://docs.rs/tokio/runtime/struct.Builder.html).

To spawn a blocking task, you should use the [ spawn_blocking](https://docs.rs/tokio/task/fn.spawn_blocking.html) function.

#[tokio::main] async fn main() { // This is running on a core thread. let blocking_task = tokio::task::spawn_blocking(|| { // This is running on a blocking thread. // Blocking here is ok. }); // We can wait for the blocking task like this: // If the blocking task panics, the unwrap below will propagate the // panic. blocking_task.await.unwrap(); }

If your code is CPU-bound and you wish to limit the number of threads used
to run it, you should run it on another thread pool such as [rayon](https://docs.rs/rayon). You
can use an [ oneshot](https://docs.rs/tokio/sync/oneshot/index.html) channel to send the result back to Tokio when the
rayon task finishes.

As well as scheduling and running tasks, Tokio provides everything you need to perform input and output asynchronously.

The [ tokio::io](https://docs.rs/tokio/io/index.html) module provides Tokio's asynchronous core I/O primitives,
the

[,](https://docs.rs/tokio/io/trait.AsyncRead.html)

`AsyncRead`[, and](https://docs.rs/tokio/io/trait.AsyncWrite.html)

`AsyncWrite`[traits. In addition, when the "io-util" feature flag is enabled, it also provides combinators and functions for working with these traits, forming as an asynchronous counterpart to](https://docs.rs/tokio/io/trait.AsyncBufRead.html)

`AsyncBufRead`[. When the "io-driver" feature flag is enabled, it also provides utilities for library authors implementing I/O resources.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/index.html)

`std::io`Tokio also includes APIs for performing various kinds of I/O and interacting with the operating system asynchronously. These include:

- `tokio::net`- [TCP](https://docs.rs/tokio/net/tcp/index.html),- [UDP](https://docs.rs/tokio/net/udp/index.html), and- [Unix Domain Sockets](https://docs.rs/tokio/net/unix/index.html)(enabled by the "net" feature flag),
- `tokio::fs`- `std::fs`
- `tokio::signal`
- `tokio::process`

A simple TCP echo server:

use tokio::net::TcpListener; use tokio::prelude::*; #[tokio::main] async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> { let mut listener = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:8080").await?; loop { let (mut socket, _) = listener.accept().await?; tokio::spawn(async move { let mut buf = [0; 1024]; // In a loop, read data from the socket and write the data back. loop { let n = match socket.read(&mut buf).await { // socket closed Ok(n) if n == 0 => return, Ok(n) => n, Err(e) => { eprintln!("failed to read from socket; err = {:?}", e); return; } }; // Write the data back if let Err(e) = socket.write_all(&buf[0..n]).await { eprintln!("failed to write to socket; err = {:?}", e); return; } } }); } }

| [fs](https://docs.rs/fs/index.html) | `fs`Asynchronous file and standard stream adaptation. |
| [io](https://docs.rs/io/index.html) | Traits, helpers, and type definitions for asynchronous I/O functionality. |
| [net](https://docs.rs/net/index.html) | TCP/UDP/Unix bindings for  |
| [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html) | A "prelude" for users of the  |
| [process](https://docs.rs/process/index.html) | `process`An implementation of asynchronous process management for Tokio. |
| [runtime](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html) | The Tokio runtime. |
| [signal](https://docs.rs/signal/index.html) | `signal`Asynchronous signal handling for Tokio |
| [stream](https://docs.rs/stream/index.html) | `stream`Stream utilities for Tokio. |
| [sync](https://docs.rs/sync/index.html) | `sync`Synchronization primitives for use in asynchronous contexts. |
| [task](https://docs.rs/task/index.html) | Asynchronous green-threads. |
| [time](https://docs.rs/time/index.html) | `time`Utilities for tracking time. |

| [join](https://docs.rs/macro.join.html) | `macros`Wait on multiple concurrent branches, returning when  |
| [pin](https://docs.rs/macro.pin.html) | Pins a value on the stack. |
| [select](https://docs.rs/macro.select.html) | `macros`Wait on multiple concurrent branches, returning when the  |
| [task_local](https://docs.rs/macro.task_local.html) | `rt-util`and`rt-core`Declares a new task-local key of type  |
| [try_join](https://docs.rs/macro.try_join.html) | `macros`Wait on multiple concurrent branches, returning when  |

| [spawn](https://docs.rs/fn.spawn.html) | `rt-core`Spawns a new asynchronous task, returning a
 |

| [main](https://docs.rs/attr.main.html) | `rt-threaded`and`macros`Marks async function to be executed by selected runtime. This macro helps set up a  |
| [test](https://docs.rs/attr.test.html) | `rt-threaded`and`macros`Marks async function to be executed by runtime, suitable to test environment |

# tokio - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tokio/^0.3.4/

A runtime for writing reliable network applications without compromising speed.

Tokio is an event-driven, non-blocking I/O platform for writing asynchronous applications with the Rust programming language. At a high level, it provides a few major components:

- Tools for [working with asynchronous tasks](https://docs.rs#working-with-tasks), including[synchronization primitives and channels](https://docs.rs/tokio/sync/index.html)and[timeouts, sleeps, and intervals](https://docs.rs/tokio/time/index.html).
- APIs for [performing asynchronous I/O](https://docs.rs#asynchronous-io), including[TCP and UDP](https://docs.rs/tokio/net/index.html)sockets,[filesystem](https://docs.rs/tokio/fs/index.html)operations, and[process](https://docs.rs/tokio/process/index.html)and[signal](https://docs.rs/tokio/signal/index.html)management.
- A [runtime](https://docs.rs/tokio/runtime/index.html)for executing asynchronous code, including a task scheduler, an I/O driver backed by the operating system's event queue (epoll, kqueue, IOCP, etc...), and a high performance timer.

Guide level documentation is found on the [website](https://tokio.rs/tokio/tutorial).

```
tokio = { version = "0.3", features = ["full"] }
```

going with `full` to ensure that you don't run into any road blocks while you're
building your application.

```

This example shows how you may want to import features for a library that just
needs to `tokio::spawn` and use a `TcpStream`.

```
tokio = { version = "0.3", features = ["rt", "net"] }
```

units of execution called [ tasks](https://docs.rs#working-with-tasks). The

[module provides important tools for working with tasks:](https://docs.rs/tokio/task/index.html)

`tokio::task`- The `spawn``JoinHandle`
- Functions for [running blocking operations](https://docs.rs/task/index.html#blocking-and-yielding)in an asynchronous task context.

The [ tokio::task](https://docs.rs/tokio/task/index.html) module is present only when the "rt" feature flag
is enabled.

The [ tokio::sync](https://docs.rs/tokio/sync/index.html) module contains synchronization primitives to use when

- channels (`oneshot``mpsc``watch`

- an asynchronous `Barrier`

The `tokio::sync` module is present only when the "sync" feature flag is

[repeating an operation at an interval](https://docs.rs/tokio/time/fn.interval.html).
